nodes.label: Seleucid Mesopotamia
nodes.full: The Greek kingdom Parthia inherited: Seleucia the megacity, the coined economy, the era count, the self-governing polis, and the temple assemblies with their observatory still running. See mesopotamia-331bc-141bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio mesopotamia-331bc-141bc.

nodes.label: Sasanian Mesopotamia
nodes.full: The empire Ardashir founds in 224 — Ctesiphon the imperial capital, the Nahrawan canal and peak agrarian wealth, a centralised tax and a Zoroastrian state church, and the rabbinic academies that redact the Babylonian Talmud. See mesopotamia-224-637.
nodes.src: background — see the folio mesopotamia-224-637.

nodes.label: Rome
nodes.full: The western empire and its legions on the Euphrates — Crassus, Trajan and the Severans invading in turn, the buyer of silk and the carrier of the plague, and the model of provincial rule that the northern plain slowly falls under.
nodes.src: background — Fergus Millar, 'The Roman Near East' (1993).

nodes.label: Han China
nodes.full: The eastern terminus of the Silk Road — the source of the silk that moved west through Parthian hands, and the court that exchanged envoys, ostrich eggs and Alexandrian conjurers with the Arsacids.
nodes.src: background — the 'Shiji' and 'Hou Hanshu'; Raoul McLaughlin (2016).

nodes.label: Roman Palestine
nodes.full: The Jewish homeland, crushed in the revolts of 66–70 and 132–135 — sending refugees and scholars east to the safe, self-governing community of Babylonia, and receiving its traffic of teachers in return.
nodes.src: background — see the folio egypt-30bc-300ad and Isaiah Gafni, 'Land, Center and Diaspora' (1997).

nodes.label: Mithridates I and the Parthian settlement
nodes.full: Mithridates I entered Seleucia in 141 and had himself acclaimed there; within a year the Babylonian Diaries were dating by 'Arsaces the king'. The Parthians kept almost everything as they found it — the Greek city and its constitution, the temple assemblies, the satrapal machinery — and added little but a garrison and a share of the revenue. It was the Achaemenid light hand a third time over.
nodes.src: The Astronomical Diaries for 141 BC; Justin XXXVI.1 and XLI.6; Josef Wiesehöfer, 'Ancient Persia' (2001).

nodes.label: Mithridates II the Great — the height of the empire
nodes.full: Mithridates II pushed the frontier to the Euphrates, brought Characene, Adiabene and Armenia to heel, took the old title 'King of Kings', and in 96 received the first Roman envoy, Sulla, on the Euphrates. In his reign the first silk caravans from Han China reached Parthian territory. After him a forty-year tangle of rival kings weakened the centre and let the vassal kingdoms grow.
nodes.src: Justin XXXVIII.3 and XLII.2; Plutarch, 'Sulla' 5; the Chinese account of Anxi in the 'Shiji' 123.

nodes.label: Orodes II — Carrhae and the wars with Rome begin
nodes.full: In 53 BC the proconsul Crassus crossed the Euphrates to conquer Parthia and was annihilated at Carrhae by a much smaller force under the general Surenas: seven legions destroyed, Crassus killed, the eagles taken. Orodes's son Pacorus then invaded Roman Syria in 40 and was thrown back and killed. The three-century contest for Mesopotamia had begun, and it would not end while either empire stood.
nodes.src: Plutarch, 'Crassus' 23–31; Cassius Dio XL.12–27; Justin XLII.4.

nodes.label: Phraates IV to Vologases I — the long stand-off
nodes.full: Phraates IV returned the captured eagles to Augustus in 20 BC and the two empires settled into an armed peace punctuated by wars over Armenia. Under Vologases I the arrangement hardened: a Parthian prince on the Armenian throne, crowned by Rome. Through these decades Seleucia rose against the crown for seven years, an autonomy the Arsacids could not simply crush.
nodes.src: 'Res Gestae Divi Augusti' 29; Tacitus, 'Annals' VI.31–44 and XV; the 'Anilaeus and Asinaeus' episode in Josephus, 'Antiquities' XVIII.9.

nodes.label: Osroes I and the Trajanic war
nodes.full: In 116 Trajan came down the Euphrates and the Tigris, took Ctesiphon, sailed to the Persian Gulf, and declared the provinces of Mesopotamia and Assyria — the one time Rome held the whole land. It collapsed at once: the cities and the Jewish diaspora rose in his rear, the garrisons were cut off, and Hadrian on his accession in 117 gave the conquest back and set the border on the Euphrates again.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio LXVIII.26–33; the 'Kitos War' in Eusebius, 'Ecclesiastical History' IV.2; Fergus Millar, 'The Roman Near East' (1993).

nodes.label: Vologases IV to Artabanus IV — the sacks and the fall
nodes.full: Twice more Roman armies burned the capital region — Avidius Cassius in 165, Septimius Severus in 198 — each time withdrawing, each time leaving the north a little more Roman. Then the blow came from within: Ardashir, the vassal king of Persis, beat the last Arsacid, Artabanus IV, on the plain of Hormozdgan in April 224. The Parthian empire was finished after four and a half centuries.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio LXXI–LXXX; Herodian VI.2; the Sasanian account in al-Tabari I (tr. Bosworth 1999).

nodes.label: Characene at the head of the Gulf
nodes.full: On the marshy delta where the rivers met the sea, an officer named Hyspaosines founded a kingdom in the wreck of the late Seleucid east, with its capital at Charax. Characene minted its own coinage for three centuries, sat astride the sea route to India, and drew the Palmyrene caravan trade to its wharves. It was the most durable of the buffer states, annexed only when Ardashir swept the Gulf in 222.
nodes.src: Pliny, 'Natural History' VI.31; Monika Schuol, 'Die Charakene' (2000); the Characene royal coin series.

nodes.label: Hatra, Edessa and Adiabene — the buffer principalities
nodes.full: Between the two empires lay a belt of small kingdoms under Arsacid overlordship: Hatra, an Arab desert city grown rich on its shrine and its position, whose walls turned back both Trajan and Severus; Edessa, the Abgarid capital where Syriac letters began; and Adiabene around Arbela, whose royal house converted to Judaism in the first century. Rome absorbed them one by one from 165 on.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio LXVIII.31 and LXXVI.10–12 (Hatra); the Adiabene conversion in Josephus, 'Antiquities' XX.2–4; Steven Ross, 'Roman Edessa' (2001).

nodes.label: Carrhae — the destruction of Crassus
nodes.full: Crassus led seven legions across the Euphrates in search of a triumph. On the open plain near Carrhae the Parthian general Surenas surrounded them with horse-archers and a camel train of spare arrows and shot them to pieces over a long day. Some twenty thousand Romans died and ten thousand were marched east as captives; the legionary eagles were carried to Ctesiphon. It was Rome's worst defeat in the East.
nodes.src: Plutarch, 'Crassus' 23–31; Cassius Dio XL.17–27.

nodes.label: The Parthian thrust into Syria and the recoil
nodes.full: With Rome in civil war the Parthians struck west: Pacorus and the Roman renegade Labienus overran Syria and pushed into Anatolia and Judaea in 40. Mark Antony's lieutenant Ventidius then beat them in three battles, killing Pacorus at Gindarus in 38 on the anniversary of Carrhae. Antony's own great invasion of 36 failed in Media with heavy loss. The frontier settled back on the Euphrates.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio XLVIII.24–27 and XLIX.19–33; Plutarch, 'Antony' 33–52.

nodes.label: The seven-year revolt of Seleucia
nodes.full: Seleucia threw off Arsacid control for seven years during a disputed succession, its Greek and Syrian citizens uniting against the crown — and, at the height of it, turning on the city's large Jewish community and massacring thousands. The Parthians recovered the city only by concession. It was the last time the old Greek megacity acted as an independent power, and the beginning of its long decline.
nodes.src: Tacitus, 'Annals' XI.8–9; Josephus, 'Antiquities' XVIII.9.8–9.

nodes.label: Trajan takes Ctesiphon, and the rear catches fire
nodes.full: Trajan stormed down the two rivers, entered Ctesiphon in 116, and reached the Gulf. Behind him every conquered city rose, and the Jewish communities of Mesopotamia, Cyrene and Egypt exploded into a war of their own. Trajan's generals retook the cities with massacres; the emperor died in 117 with the campaign unravelling, and Hadrian abandoned the whole eastern conquest within months.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio LXVIII.28–33; Eusebius, 'Ecclesiastical History' IV.2; the papyrological evidence for the diaspora revolt.

nodes.label: The burning of Seleucia in the war of Verus
nodes.full: Answering a Parthian move on Syria, Roman armies under Avidius Cassius drove to the Tigris. Seleucia opened its gates and was sacked and burned anyway — a betrayal the sources note — and the palace at Ctesiphon was levelled. The great Greek city never recovered. The returning legions carried a pestilence, the Antonine Plague, that killed for a decade across the whole Roman world.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio LXXI.2; the 'Historia Augusta', 'Lucius Verus' 8; on the plague, Galen and R. J. Littman & M. L. Littman (1973).

nodes.label: The Severan sacks and the Sasanian revolt
nodes.full: Septimius Severus sacked Ctesiphon in 198, enslaved a hundred thousand, and made the north a Roman province — but failed twice under the walls of Hatra. Caracalla attacked again in 216 and was murdered. Then Ardashir, king of Persis, rose against his Arsacid overlord and destroyed Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan in 224. Two years later he took Ctesiphon and the Sasanian age began.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio LXXV–LXXIX; Herodian VI.2; al-Tabari I (tr. Bosworth 1999).

nodes.label: The King of Kings and the great houses
nodes.full: The Arsacid empire was a confederation, not a state. The King of Kings held the centre and the road; around him a handful of noble clans — the Suren, the Karin and the rest — held hereditary offices and armies, and a ring of vassal kings ran their own affairs and coinage. There was no salaried bureaucracy and no standing army beyond the royal guard. It worked for four centuries and left the Sasanians much to centralise.
nodes.src: Josef Wiesehöfer, 'Ancient Persia' (2001); the noble houses in the 'Letter of Tansar' and al-Tabari.

nodes.label: Ctesiphon rises across the river from Seleucia
nodes.full: The Arsacids did not live in Greek Seleucia; they built their own residence on the east bank opposite it, and Ctesiphon grew from an army camp into the winter capital of the empire and the largest city of the region. The two settlements and their neighbours eventually fused into the sprawl the Arabs would call al-Madā'in, 'the Cities' — the seat of empire for the next eight hundred years.
nodes.src: Strabo XVI.1.16; Pliny VI.30; Jens Kröger, 'Ctesiphon' in Encyclopaedia Iranica.

nodes.label: Seleucia keeps its Greek constitution
nodes.full: Under Parthian suzerainty Seleucia went on governing itself as a Greek polis: an elected council, annual magistrates, its own bronze coinage stamped 'of the autonomous Seleucians', and years still counted on the Seleucid era. A Greek civic island inside an Iranian empire, it kept the arrangement for three centuries — until the Roman sack of 165 broke it for good.
nodes.src: the autonomous coinage of Seleucia; Tacitus, 'Annals' VI.42; Getzel Cohen, 'The Hellenistic Settlements in the East' (2013).

nodes.label: The temple assemblies still meet
nodes.full: The Esagila kept its assembly, its administrator and its accounts under the Parthians as under everyone before. A cluster of tablets from the 90s BC — the Rahimesu archive — shows the temple still collecting its rents and offerings and still dealing with a royal official who took his cut. The institution that had run Babylon's inner life since the Bronze Age was in its last generations, but it was still running.
nodes.src: the Rahimesu archive (CT 49); R. J. van der Spek, 'The Šatammus of Esagila in the Seleucid and Arsacid Periods' (2000).

nodes.label: Two eras on the same tablet
nodes.full: Parthian rule changed the dating formulae and little else: scribes now wrote the year twice, once on the old Seleucid count and once on the Arsacid era that ran from 247 BC, and named 'Arsaces' alongside the reigning king. The law, the contracts, the temple calendar and the units of measure all carried on. The lightest of overlordships, laid over institutions a thousand years deep.
nodes.src: the double-dated Late Babylonian tablets; Gerd Gropp on the Arsacid era.

nodes.label: From clay to parchment and potsherd
nodes.full: As cuneiform faded, the region's paperwork moved onto perishable stuff — Aramaic deeds on parchment and papyrus, receipts on broken pottery, a few in Greek. The bilingual parchments from Avroman in the Zagros, a vineyard sale of 88 BC among them, show the new practice already fixed. Most of it has rotted; the clay tablets survive precisely because their medium was obsolete.
nodes.src: the Avroman parchments (E. H. Minns, JHS 1915); Sebastian Brock on the earliest Syriac legal documents.

nodes.label: The last cuneiform tablet
nodes.full: The youngest cuneiform tablet that can be dated is an astronomical almanac computed for the Seleucid year equivalent to AD 79/80, written in the Esagila. After it the wedge-script — three thousand years of kings, contracts, prayers, omens and star-tables — simply stops. A handful of scholars kept reading the old tablets for a while longer; no one wrote new ones.
nodes.src: Hermann Hunger & Teije de Jong, 'Almanac W22340a from Uruk: The Latest Datable Cuneiform Tablet' (ZA 2014); M. J. Geller, 'The Last Wedge' (1997).

nodes.label: The exilarch and the first Babylonian rabbis
nodes.full: The Arsacids recognised a head of the Jewish community — the exilarch, claiming descent from David — who held courts, levied dues and represented the Jews to the crown. Around him the first Babylonian teachers appear: Judah ben Bathyra with a school at Nisibis, a steady traffic of scholars to and from Judaea. The autonomy and the learning that would make Babylonia the centre of the Jewish world were taking shape.
nodes.src: Josephus, 'Antiquities' XVIII and XX; Isaiah Gafni, 'The Jews of Babylonia in the Talmudic Era' (1990); Jacob Neusner, 'A History of the Jews in Babylonia' vol. I (1965).

nodes.label: The first churches at Edessa and Adiabene
nodes.full: Christianity entered Mesopotamia early, moving along the trade roads and through the synagogues of the Aramaic-speaking towns. Edessa had a church and a bishop by the later second century, with the philosopher Bardaisan at the royal court; Adiabene and the district of Arbela had communities too. It was the first Christianity to grow up entirely outside the Roman Empire, in Syriac from the start.
nodes.src: the 'Chronicle of Edessa'; Sebastian Brock, 'The Church of the East in the Sasanian Empire' (2000); Walter Bauer on Edessene Christianity.

nodes.label: Bel, Nabu and Nanaya carry on
nodes.full: The old cults outlasted their script. Marduk was still honoured at Babylon and was carried by merchants to Palmyra, where he got a great temple as Bel; Nabu kept his at Borsippa; and at Uruk a Parthian-style temple to Nanaya and her consort Gareus was built as late as 110 AD. The gods were taking Hellenised and Aramaic forms, but the sanctuaries of the third millennium were still receiving offerings.
nodes.src: the Gareus temple at Uruk; the cult of Bel at Palmyra (dedicated AD 32); Michael Sommer, 'Palmyra' (2018).

nodes.label: Hatra of Shamash
nodes.full: Hatra was in effect a temple-state: a vast circular sanctuary at the centre of the walled city, dedicated to the sun god Shamash and the triad the inscriptions call Our Lord, Our Lady and the Son of Our Lord, drawing pilgrims and offerings from the whole steppe. The wealth of the shrine paid for the walls that twice turned back Rome. When the Sasanians finally took the city around 240 they left it to the desert.
nodes.src: the Hatran Aramaic inscriptions; Lucinda Dirven (ed.), 'Hatra: Politics, Culture and Religion between Parthia and Rome' (2013).

nodes.label: The baptising sects of the lower canals
nodes.full: The marshy canal country south of Ctesiphon bred a cluster of baptising sects — communities that practised repeated ritual immersion and mixed Jewish, Christian, Iranian and old Babylonian ideas. Mani, born there in 216 into an Elchasaite group, would grow up inside this world before breaking with it. The Mandaeans, who survive on those same rivers today, trace their beginnings to it.
nodes.src: the 'Cologne Mani Codex'; Kevin van Bladel, 'From Sasanian Mandaeans to Ṣābians of the Marshes' (2017).

nodes.label: The last colophons in cuneiform
nodes.full: In the temple schools of Babylon and Uruk a shrinking circle of scholars kept copying the star-tables, the omen series and the classics, signing each tablet with a colophon that named the copyist and his teacher. The Graeco-Babyloniaca exercises — cuneiform on one side, Greek letters on the other — are from these last generations. When the copying ended the written culture of ancient Mesopotamia ended with it.
nodes.src: Philippe Clancier, 'Les bibliothèques en Babylonie' (2009); the Graeco-Babyloniaca in M. J. Geller (1997).

nodes.label: Syriac becomes a written language
nodes.full: The Aramaic dialect of Edessa began to be written in its own cursive script — the earliest dated example is a tomb inscription of AD 6 — and by the early third century it had legal documents, a Bible translation in progress, and Bardaisan's dialogue on fate and free will, the first work of Syriac prose. This local literature would carry Christianity across Persia, Central Asia and India.
nodes.src: H. J. W. Drijvers & J. F. Healey, 'The Old Syriac Inscriptions of Edessa and Osrhoene' (1999); Bardaisan, 'The Book of the Laws of Countries'.

nodes.label: Parthian frontality
nodes.full: Parthian art turned its figures to face the viewer head-on, standing stiff and symmetrical, eyes forward — gods, kings and donors alike. It is everywhere at Hatra and Dura-Europos, in stone, stucco and paint. The convention spread west into Roman provincial sculpture and, through it, into the frontal saints and Christs of Byzantine and medieval art. A Mesopotamian way of showing the sacred outlived the empire that made it.
nodes.src: Daniel Schlumberger, 'L'Orient hellénisé' (1970); Malcolm Colledge, 'Parthian Art' (1977).

nodes.label: The showcase cities in stone and stucco
nodes.full: The Parthian centuries left a distinctive built decoration: the carved stone statues and temple facades of Hatra, the moulded gypsum stucco that sheathed the walls at reoccupied Assur and at Ctesiphon, and the mass-produced terracottas and stamped sealings still turned out at Seleucia. The vocabulary mixed Greek acanthus, Iranian motifs and Semitic dress into something the region had not made before.
nodes.src: Walter Andrae & Heinz Lenzen, 'Die Partherstadt Assur' (1933); Antonio Invernizzi on Seleucia.

nodes.label: The Chaldean handbooks in Greek
nodes.full: By the Roman imperial period 'Chaldean' astrology circulated as Greek textbooks — the works going under the name of Teucer of Babylon among them — laying out the zodiac, the decans, the rising-times and the readings. The Babylonian doctrine had been fully absorbed into a Mediterranean science, and Babylon itself had become its legendary home rather than its working centre.
nodes.src: Franz Boll, 'Sphaera' (1903); Tamsyn Barton, 'Ancient Astrology' (1994).

nodes.label: The observatory winds down
nodes.full: The Esagila scholars kept up the nightly watch and the predictive almanacs into the first century AD, then stopped. Roman writers still named the Babylonians Naburimannu and Kidinnu as the founders of the lunar theories the whole world now used. Two and a half millennia of continuous sky-records — the longest scientific project in history — reached its end here, quietly, for want of successors.
nodes.src: Pliny, 'Natural History' II.6; the latest Diaries and almanacs in Sachs & Hunger and in Hunger & de Jong (2014).

nodes.label: Ptolemy builds the Almagest on Babylonian data
nodes.full: Ptolemy's 'Almagest', the book that fixed astronomy for fourteen centuries, rests on a Babylonian footing: eclipse observations reaching back to 721 BC, the sexagesimal number system, the 360-degree circle, and the period relations for the moon and planets — most of it reaching him through Hipparchus. The Mesopotamian achievement was now embedded in the Greek synthesis that would carry it forward.
nodes.src: G. J. Toomer (tr.), 'Ptolemy's Almagest' (1984); Alexander Jones, 'The Adaptation of Babylonian Methods in Greek Numerical Astronomy' (1991).

nodes.label: Astrology becomes a universal science
nodes.full: By the imperial period the horoscope was cast from Roman Britain to India, and its framework — the zodiac, the twelve places, the aspects, the planetary rulerships — was Babylonian to the core, refined by Greek geometry. Mesopotamia was remembered as its birthplace even as its own practitioners fell silent. It is the most widely practised legacy of ancient Babylon, and still is.
nodes.src: Dorotheus of Sidon, 'Carmen Astrologicum'; Vettius Valens, 'Anthologiae'; Francesca Rochberg, 'In the Path of the Moon' (2010).

nodes.label: The oral Torah moves east
nodes.full: After the destruction of Jerusalem the centre of Jewish life began shifting toward the large, secure, self-governing community of Babylonia. Scholars carried the mishnaic material and the methods of legal argument to the schools of Nisibis and Nehardea, and a two-way traffic of teachers ran with Palestine. By the end of the Parthian period Babylonia was poised to become the senior seat of the law and produce the Talmud that bears its name.
nodes.src: Jacob Neusner, 'A History of the Jews in Babylonia' vol. I (1965); Isaiah Gafni, 'Land, Center and Diaspora' (1997).

nodes.label: The exorcist's craft outlives the script
nodes.full: The lore of the Babylonian āšipu — the incantations, the protective figurines, the demon-names Lilith and Lamashtu, the rites against sickness and the evil eye — did not stop when cuneiform did. It passed into the Aramaic magical practice of Jews, Mandaeans and Christians in the same towns, and surfaces a few centuries later on the inscribed clay bowls buried under house floors across Iraq.
nodes.src: Markham Geller, 'Ancient Babylonian Medicine' (2010); Shaul Shaked & others, 'Aramaic Bowl Spells' (2013– ).

nodes.label: The emporium of the East
nodes.full: The cluster of cities at the Tigris crossing — Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and the royal foundation of Vologesias — was where the caravan roads from Syria, Iran, Arabia and Central Asia met the river down to the Gulf. Everything moving between the Mediterranean and Asia passed through, and the tolls on it were one of the crown's largest revenues. Pliny still called Seleucia the trading capital of the East.
nodes.src: Pliny, 'Natural History' VI.30 and VI.122; Nikolaus Schindel on Arsacid fiscal structure.

nodes.label: Parthia the Silk Road middleman
nodes.full: Parthia sat between the Roman and Han empires and made sure they never traded direct. Chinese silk moved west and Roman glass, wool and gold moved east, all through Parthian hands and at a Parthian mark-up. When the Han envoy Gan Ying reached the Persian Gulf in 97 meaning to sail to Rome, Parthian sailors talked him out of it with tales of a voyage that could take years. The monopoly was the point.
nodes.src: the 'Hou Hanshu' 88 (Gan Ying); Raoul McLaughlin, 'The Roman Empire and the Silk Routes' (2016).

nodes.label: Characene and the Palmyrene sea trade
nodes.full: Charax, the Characene capital at the river mouth, was the transit port for goods coming up from India, and the merchants of Palmyra ran the business: they kept trading colonies at Charax, Vologesias and Forat, financed and led the caravans across the desert, and set up statues at home to the men who brought them back. One Palmyrene even served as a Characene official on the island of Tylos.
nodes.src: the Palmyrene caravan inscriptions (PAT); the 'Palmyra Tariff' (AD 137); Michael Sommer, 'Palmyra' (2018).

nodes.label: The agrarian base still rich
nodes.full: Under the light Parthian hand the canal country stayed productive and populous — grain, dates, wool, and the bitumen springs at Hit that caulked the region's boats. Settlement drifted with the rivers, some old land going dry as the Tigris moved east toward Ctesiphon. The great state canal-building that would push output higher still was left for the Sasanians; the Parthians lived off what they inherited.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Land Behind Baghdad' (1965); Robert Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981).

nodes.label: The Arsacid drachm and the Seleucia tetradrachm
nodes.full: The empire ran on the silver drachm with the seated archer, struck in vast numbers, and on the dated tetradrachms of the Seleucia mint, which ran without a break for three centuries and give historians their firmest Parthian chronology. The silver was steadily debased as the reigns went on. Characene struck its own coins to the end, a mark of how real its independence was.
nodes.src: David Sellwood, 'An Introduction to the Coinage of Parthia' (1980); Fred Shore, 'Parthian Coins and History' (1993).

nodes.label: The palaces of Ctesiphon
nodes.full: Ctesiphon's royal quarter was built in mudbrick and fired brick on a scale to match its role as the winter seat of the King of Kings — audience halls, courts and the sprawling administrative buildings that made it the largest city of the region. The Parthian works are largely lost under the later Sasanian rebuilding, but the ambition and the vaulted style that produced the great arch of Ctesiphon began here.
nodes.src: Oscar Reuther, 'Die Ausgrabungen der deutschen Ktesiphon-Expedition' (1930); Jens Kröger in Encyclopaedia Iranica.

nodes.label: The iwan
nodes.full: The Parthians developed the iwan — a deep hall, barrel-vaulted, standing wide open at one end — and made it the monumental centrepiece of palace and temple. The earliest grand examples are at Parthian Assur and at Hatra. From there it became the defining element of Mesopotamian and Iranian architecture: the Sasanian throne hall, the mosque, the madrasa and the courtyard house all turn on it.
nodes.src: Walter Andrae & Heinz Lenzen, 'Die Partherstadt Assur' (1933); Lionel Bier, 'The Iwan' in Encyclopaedia Iranica.

nodes.label: Vault, squinch and gypsum
nodes.full: Building in a land with no timber for centering, Parthian masons laid the barrel vault in tilted slices that each stood on the last, roofed square rooms with domes carried on corner squinches, and bedded it all in gypsum mortar that set in minutes. The technique made large vaulted halls cheap and fast. Hatra, with good limestone to hand, is the outlier — cut ashlar and true arches.
nodes.src: K. A. C. Creswell, 'Early Muslim Architecture' vol. I (1969), on the antecedents; the Assur and Ctesiphon vaulting.

nodes.label: The rivers on the move
nodes.full: The Tigris was shifting its main bed eastward, toward Ctesiphon — feeding the new capital's growth while the old Euphrates cities, Babylon among them, lost water and shrank. The Parthians kept the existing canals in repair but attempted no grand new works. The engineering answer to a floodplain whose rivers would not hold still was postponed to the Sasanian Nahrawan.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); Hermann Gasche & others on the Tigris channel shifts.

nodes.label: The land between Rome and Parthia
nodes.full: For nearly three centuries Mesopotamia was the debated ground of two empires — raided, invaded, ruled by neither. The border crept east: the Euphrates line held until the 160s, then Rome took the northern plain after 198 and made it the province of Mesopotamia with its capital at Nisibis. Caravan towns like Dura-Europos changed hands again and again. It is the original of the Roman–Persian frontier that outlasted both dynasties.
nodes.src: Fergus Millar, 'The Roman Near East, 31 BC – AD 337' (1993); the Dura-Europos excavation archive.

nodes.label: Palmyra's network down the Euphrates
nodes.full: Palmyra, on the desert edge, built a commercial reach that ran deep into Parthian territory: agents and temples at Vologesias, Seleucia and Charax, caravans it organised, armed and insured, and a famous tariff law of 137 fixing the dues on everything from slaves to perfume. Palmyrene, a dialect of Aramaic, and Greek stood side by side on the honorific statues of its merchant princes.
nodes.src: the 'Palmyra Tariff' (AD 137, now in the Hermitage); the Palmyrene caravan texts in D. Schlumberger and J. Cantineau.

nodes.label: Embassies to and from Han China
nodes.full: From the time of Mithridates II, Parthian and Chinese courts exchanged envoys along the newly opened Silk Road; the Chinese records note gifts of ostrich eggs and 'jugglers from Alexandria' sent east. When Rome tried to reach past Parthia — the envoy Gan Ying in 97, later merchants calling themselves 'from Daqin' — the Parthians made sure the through route stayed closed and the profit stayed theirs.
nodes.src: the 'Shiji' 123 and 'Hou Hanshu' 88 and 118; Yu Taishan on Han–Parthian contacts.

nodes.label: The Jewish tie to Palestine
nodes.full: Babylonian and Palestinian Jewry stayed one people across the frontier: pilgrims and the Temple tax before 70, a constant traffic of scholars, and a settled tradition that certain families and towns went back to the first exile. Each Roman crushing of a revolt — 70, 116, 135 — sent refugees east and left the Babylonian community relatively larger, safer and more central than before.
nodes.src: Isaiah Gafni, 'Land, Center and Diaspora: Jewish Constructs in Late Antiquity' (1997); the conversion of Adiabene in Josephus, 'Antiquities' XX.

nodes.label: The Christian mission along the roads
nodes.full: Christianity moved east along the same caravan roads and through the same Aramaic-speaking towns as the Jewish network — from Edessa into Adiabene and down to Ctesiphon, in Syriac from the start, often planted first among the Jews of a place. Bardaisan of Edessa already had an interest in the Christians of India. The Church of the East that would reach China was taking its first steps in Parthian Iraq.
nodes.src: J. M. Fiey, 'Jalons pour une histoire de l'Église en Iraq' (1970); Sebastian Brock, 'The Church of the East in the Sasanian Empire' (2000).

nodes.label: The land between the empires
nodes.full: For the first time in its history Mesopotamia was a permanent borderland — fought over by Rome and Parthia, fully ruled by neither, its cities changing masters and its north slowly turning Roman. The condition outlasted both dynasties: the same frontier, in the same country, divided Rome from Sasanian Persia and then Byzantium from the Caliphate. Iraq as a contested edge rather than a centre begins here.
nodes.src: Fergus Millar, 'The Roman Near East' (1993); Josef Wiesehöfer, 'Ancient Persia' (2001).

nodes.label: The Aramaic renaissance
nodes.full: With Greek shrinking back to Seleucia and cuneiform dead, the local forms of Aramaic came into their own as written languages — Syriac at Edessa, Jewish Babylonian Aramaic in the south, Mandaic on the marsh rivers, the Hatran dialect in the steppe. This was not a survival of something old but the making of something new: the linguistic and literary map of late antique Iraq.
nodes.src: John Healey, 'The Edessan Milieu and the Birth of Syriac' (2007); Michael Sokoloff's Aramaic dictionaries.

nodes.label: The three religions strike root
nodes.full: By the end of the Parthian period the same Mesopotamian cities held rabbinic Jewish communities with their own courts, the first Syriac Christian congregations, and the still-living cults of Bel, Nanaya and Shamash — arguing, converting and competing in the same streets. The religious landscape of late antique and early Islamic Iraq, layered and plural, was seeded in these two centuries.
nodes.src: Jacob Neusner, 'A History of the Jews in Babylonia' (1965–70); Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984), on the deep background.

nodes.label: The Parthian template
nodes.full: The Arsacid way of holding Mesopotamia was the lightest yet: vassal kings left in place, the Greek city self-governing, the temple assemblies untouched, the languages and laws alone, the crown taking the road-tolls and the tribute and little else. The Sasanians kept the outward shape — a King of Kings at Ctesiphon — but pulled the tax, the army and the official religion back into the centre.
nodes.src: Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984); Touraj Daryaee, 'Sasanian Persia' (2009).

nodes.label: The last scribe of the Esagila
nodes.full: An old man of a priestly house, one of the few left who could still write the wedge-script, ruling the lines for an astronomical almanac as his father and grandfather had. The apprentice at his side was learning Aramaic and a little Greek and would never use cuneiform for anything. When men like him died, a profession three thousand years old died with them, and the tablets became unreadable objects.
nodes.src: the latest datable tablets in Hunger & de Jong (2014); Philippe Clancier (2009) on the last scholars.

nodes.label: The exilarch at the Arsacid court
nodes.full: The head of Babylonian Jewry — the exilarch, who traced his line to King David — rode to the King of Kings as a recognised prince of his people, judged their disputes, appointed their judges, collected their taxes, and kept the genealogies that said who was of pure descent. The office, and the self-government it embodied, is why the community could become the anchor of the Jewish world.
nodes.src: the exilarchate in Neusner vol. I–II (1965–66); M. Beer, 'The Babylonian Exilarchate' (Hebrew, 1970).

nodes.label: The Palmyrene caravan chief at Charax
nodes.full: He put up the money, hired the guards and the camels, and led the round trip from Palmyra across the desert to Charax and on by ship toward the Indus, then home with the pepper and the pearls. If the caravan came back whole, the merchants he had carried clubbed together to raise his statue in Palmyra's colonnade, with an inscription in Palmyrene and Greek listing what he had spent and risked.
nodes.src: the Palmyrene caravan honorifics (PAT 0294 and others); Michael Sommer, 'Palmyra' (2018).

nodes.label: The Christian of Edessa
nodes.full: A dyer or a merchant in the first city to have a church outside the Roman world, he heard the gospel as a single woven narrative — Tatian's harmony — in his own Syriac, not in Greek or Latin. In the colonnades he might argue free will and the power of the stars with the students of Bardaisan, the Christian philosopher who sat at the king's table. His faith would travel the trade roads east for a thousand years.
nodes.src: the 'Doctrine of Addai'; H. J. W. Drijvers, 'Bardaisan of Edessa' (1966).

nodes.label: The Parthian nobleman
nodes.full: A lord of one of the great clans, he owed the King of Kings armoured cavalry service, not taxes; he ran his estates through stewards, hunted, and kept a household that outshone some vassal kings. His tomb relief showed him full-face, stiff and bejewelled, in the trousered Parthian dress — the frontal style that would end up on the walls of churches. Power in this empire ran through men like him, not through an office.
nodes.src: the noble houses in the 'Letter of Tansar' and al-Tabari; the Parthian funerary reliefs of Assur (Andrae & Lenzen 1933).
